newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe to announce crucial budget.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe to announce crucial budget.

text.p: Zimbabwe announces a crucial budget on Thursday in which key Western donors expect the government to tackle a perennially high deficit to help it win donor funding for economic reforms.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank say the budget by Finance Minister Herbert Murerwa will determine how soon the two institutions will resume financial aid suspended two years ago over missed economic targets.
The 1997/98 budget is due at 1330 GMT and will cover 18 months from this month to enable the southern African country to align its financial year to the calendar year in 1999.

There is widespread speculation that President Robert Mugabe's cash-strapped government may raise taxes on fuel, consumer sales tax and or even introduce a new land tax to boost its coffers, under pressure lately from an annual round of pay rises of over 30 percent.
Mugabe streamlined his cabinet hours before the Thursday budget, axing three ministries and merging others in what officials said was an attempt to cut back state spending as demanded by aid donors.

The IMF and the World Bank have said they will study the budget and discuss with Zimbabwe in September its bid for support for a new phase of economic reforms which the country plans to launch later this year.

They will be looking specifically at measures to cut state spending, which accounts for about 38 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and is seen by many as supporting a political patronage system.

Both institutions supported Zimbabwe's first five-year economic structural adjustment programme (ESAP), but they withdrew before it ended in 1995 when Mugabe's government -- whose budget deficit has averaged 10 percent of GDP annually over the past 10 years -- missed some cost-saving targets.
The second phase of ESAP has been put on hold pending progress on the budget deficit, and other issues such as reducing inflation and speeding up privatisation.

Zimbabwe's annual inflation edged up to 21.4 percent in June from 20.7 percent in May, against a target of 16 percent. Local economic analysts expect it to rise to 24 percent in the last two quarters of the year, fuelled by high money supply growth and expected hikes in excise duties.

Murerwa told Reuters early this month that he expected the budget deficit for the financial year ended June 30 to be around 10.3 percent, way off a target of 8.5 percent. Zimbabwe also missed its deficit target of 6.7 percent in 1995/96, hitting 10.1 percent.
